result:
Here’s a small piece on something ordinary and endlessly interesting: windows.

A window is a strange object. It is not quite inside and not quite outside. It belongs to a wall, but it refuses to behave like one. A wall says no; a window says maybe. Through it, the world becomes available in portions: a slice of sky, a passing tree, rain changing the color of a street, a face pausing for a second in the glass.

We often think of windows as things for looking out of, but they also let light in, and that changes a room more than furniture ever could. Light makes an ordinary table look deliberate. It can turn dust into weather. It can make silence visible. In the morning, a window can feel generous. At night, it becomes reflective, and the room stares back at us.

There’s also something quietly hopeful about windows. Even when they are closed, they imply access. They suggest that the world is larger than the room we’re in, that beyond the immediate moment there are streets, seasons, people, accidents, and weather continuing without our permission. A window is proof that separation does not have to mean isolation.

And yet, windows can be melancholy too. Anyone who has watched a city from behind glass knows that clarity and distance can exist together. You can see everything and still not be part of it. That is one of the oldest human feelings: being near a thing and unable to touch it.

Maybe that’s why windows appear so often in stories, paintings, and memories. They are threshold objects. They help us imagine change. A person at a window is usually waiting, remembering, or deciding. The frame divides the scene into something that can be held in attention. It tells us: look here. This matters.

I like that windows do their work quietly. They do not announce themselves. They simply allow. In a world full of doors, locks, and alarms, that feels almost radical.

If you want, I can also write something more whimsical, more philosophical, or completely different.
